title: Check yourself: choosing and combining functional interfaces

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A library declares `interface Matcher { boolean matches(String s); boolean equals(Object o); int hashCode(); default Matcher negate() { return s -> !matches(s); } }`, with no annotation. What does javac do with `Matcher m = s -> s.isBlank();`?

options.text: It compiles it, since equals and hashCode are public methods of Object, which leaves matches as the one method to supply
options.says: abstract redeclarations of Object's public methods don't count, so one abstract method is left

options.text: It compiles it, since a lambda supplies the first abstract method of an interface and the other two are left unimplemented
options.says: a lambda can only target an interface with exactly one abstract method left; there is no 'first method' rule

options.text: It rejects it, since equals and hashCode are declared abstract here, which makes three methods the lambda would have to supply
options.says: Comparator also redeclares equals and is functional: Object's public methods are set aside

options.text: It rejects it, since Matcher carries no @FunctionalInterface, which an interface needs before a lambda can target it
options.says: the annotation only makes javac check the interface; an unannotated interface with one abstract method takes a lambda

origin.section: One Abstract Method Makes an Interface Functional; @FunctionalInterface Only Checks It

questions.stem: `PaymentHook` has one abstract method and no annotation. Services in three other repositories implement it with lambdas. A developer adds `void rollback(String id)` to it and builds the repository that declares it, which holds no lambda for it. What does that build report?

options.text: No error here, and the services fail when they are next compiled, since the interface on its own is still valid Java
options.says: without the annotation the interface compiles; the error appears where each lambda is compiled

options.text: No error here, and the services keep compiling, since each lambda compiled against PaymentHook gets an empty rollback
options.says: no method is filled in: each service's next build fails with 'not a functional interface'

options.text: An error here, and the services keep compiling, since javac checks the interface against the lambdas in other repositories
options.says: javac sees only what it compiles; the interface alone compiles

options.text: An error here, and the services fail too, since an interface may add an abstract method only when it supplies a default
options.says: an interface may declare any number of abstract methods; only the annotation makes javac reject a second one

origin.section: One Abstract Method Makes an Interface Functional; @FunctionalInterface Only Checks It

questions.stem: A team declares `@FunctionalInterface interface Slugger { String slug(String title); }` and `Slugger kebab = t -> t.toLowerCase().replace(' ', '-');`. A library method `normalise(Function<String, String> f)` should run kebab's logic. Which call works?

options.text: `normalise(kebab::slug)`, since a method reference can target any functional interface whose method fits slug
options.says: a method reference can target Function; Slugger itself is not a Function

options.text: `normalise(kebab)`, since a Slugger value is accepted where a Function is expected when their shapes match
options.says: same shape doesn't relate the types: 'Slugger cannot be converted to Function<String,String>'

options.text: `normalise((Function<String, String>) kebab)`, since the cast makes the lambda object implement Function as well
options.says: the cast compiles, but the object is only a Slugger, so it throws ClassCastException

options.text: `normalise(Function.<String>identity().andThen(kebab))`, since andThen wraps its argument in a Function whose apply calls slug
options.says: andThen takes a Function, and a Slugger is not one, so this doesn't compile

origin.section: Use java.util.function Until a Name, a Checked Exception or a Third Parameter Asks for Your Own

questions.stem: A rules engine applies `Function<Integer, Integer>` steps to amounts in cents, mostly between 1,000 and 50,000. Twenty different step lambdas go through the one `step.apply(amount)` call in the engine's loop. On a warmed-up JVM, what does an allocation profiler show for that call?

options.text: Two Integer objects per call, since twenty lambdas at one call site keep the JIT from inlining them and removing the boxing
options.says: with three lambdas through one call site the run allocated two 16-byte Integers per call

options.text: Two Integer objects per call, since amounts above the Integer cache are boxed into new objects on every call
options.says: with one lambda the JIT removed the boxing of values far above the cache: 28 KB for ten million calls

options.text: Almost no Integer objects, since amounts up to 50,000 fall inside the range that Integer.valueOf caches
options.says: the Integer cache covers only -128 to 127

options.text: Almost no Integer objects, since twenty lambdas are few enough for the JIT to inline every one of them in the warmed-up loop
options.says: three lambdas through one call site were already enough to stop the inlining

origin.section: Function<Integer, Integer> Boxes Each Value Unless the JIT Removes It; IntUnaryOperator Never Boxes

questions.stem: A utility declares `static <T> List<T> keep(List<T> items, Predicate<T> test)`. A caller has `List<Long> ids` and a shared `Predicate<Number> positive = n -> n.doubleValue() > 0`. What does javac do with `keep(ids, positive)`?

options.text: It rejects the call, since T would have to be Long for the list and Number for the predicate at once
options.says: inference variable T has incompatible equality constraints Number,Long; Predicate<? super T> would accept it

options.text: It rejects the call, since a Predicate<Number> has no way to test a Long it is handed
options.says: a Long is a Number, so the predicate could test it; the signature, not the predicate, is the problem

options.text: It accepts the call, since it infers T as Number, a type both arguments fit
options.says: a List<Long> is not a List<Number>, so T = Number doesn't fit the list

options.text: It accepts the call, since Long extends Number, which makes Predicate<Number> a subtype of Predicate<Long>
options.says: generic types are invariant: only a wildcard such as Predicate<? super Long> relates them

origin.section: Accept Function<? super T, ? extends R>, or Callers' Functions Don't Fit

concepts: @FunctionalInterface doesn't make an interface a lambda target; it makes javac reject a second abstract method at the interface, where without it the error appears only where a lambda targets it.
Function<Integer, Integer> allocates two Integers per call wherever the JIT can't inline the lambda, as at a call site that sees several lambdas; the primitive specialisations never box.

An interface is functional when exactly one abstract method is left after default and static methods and abstract redeclarations of Object's public methods, so Comparator, which also declares equals, is functional.
Two functional interfaces of the same shape are unrelated types: a value of one can't be passed as the other, and needs an adapter such as a method reference.
A method that takes Function<T, R> rejects a Function<Object, String> for a List<Integer>; Function<? super T, ? extends R> accepts it.
